draft.title: Integrals giving logarithms
card: The integral of 1/x is ln|x| + C. The absolute value bars are there because 1/x is defined for negative x too, but ln is only defined for positive numbers.
More generally, if the top of a fraction is the derivative of the bottom, the integral is ln|bottom| + C. In symbols: ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C.
Worked example: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx. The derivative of x² + 1 is 2x, which is the top. So the answer is ln(x² + 1) + C. Here x² + 1 is always positive, so the bars are not needed.

If the top is only a constant multiple of the derivative, take the constant out. For ∫ 3/(3x + 5) dx, the derivative of 3x + 5 is 3, so the answer is ln|3x + 5| + C. For ∫ 1/(3x + 5) dx, the top is 1, which is 1/3 of 3, so the answer is (1/3) ln|3x + 5| + C.
draft.remember: Top is the derivative of the bottom: the integral is ln|bottom| + C.

a.why: The derivative of x⁴ + 7 is 4x³, which is exactly the top, so the answer is ln(x⁴ + 7) + C. Multiplying by 4 is wrong because the 4 is already part of the derivative and is not an extra factor.
a.clue: Differentiate the bottom and compare it with the top.

b.why: The derivative of 2x + 1 is 2, but the top is only 1, which is half of 2. So the answer is (1/2) ln(2x + 1) + C. Check by differentiating: (1/2) × 2/(2x + 1) = 1/(2x + 1). Leaving out the 1/2 is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: Differentiate your answer: do you get back 1/(2x + 1)?

final.title: Integrals giving logarithms
card: The integral of \(\frac{1}{x}\) is \(\ln|x| + C\). The absolute value bars are there because \(\frac{1}{x}\) is defined for negative \(x\) too, but \(\ln\) is only defined for positive numbers.
More generally, if the top of a fraction is the derivative of the bottom, the integral is \(\ln|\text{bottom}| + C\). In symbols: \(\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \, dx = \ln|f(x)| + C\).

Worked example: \(\int \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 1} \, dx\). The derivative of \(x^{2} + 1\) is \(2x\), which is the top. So the answer is \(\ln(x^{2} + 1) + C\). Here \(x^{2} + 1\) is always positive, so the bars are not needed.

If the top is only a constant multiple of the derivative, take the constant out. For \(\int \frac{3}{3x + 5} \, dx\), the derivative of \(3x + 5\) is 3, so the answer is \(\ln|3x + 5| + C\). For \(\int \frac{1}{3x + 5} \, dx\), the top is 1, which is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of 3, so the answer is \(\frac{1}{3} \ln|3x + 5| + C\).
final.remember: Top is the derivative of the bottom: the integral is \(\ln|\text{bottom}| + C\).

a.why: The derivative of \(x^{4} + 7\) is \(4x^{3}\), which is exactly the top, so the answer is \(\ln(x^{4} + 7) + C\). Multiplying by 4 is wrong because the 4 is already part of the derivative and is not an extra factor.
a.clue: Differentiate the bottom and compare it with the top.

b.why: The derivative of \(2x + 1\) is 2, but the top is only 1, which is half of 2. So the answer is \(\frac{1}{2} \ln(2x + 1) + C\). Check by differentiating: \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{2x + 1} = \frac{1}{2x + 1}\). Leaving out the \(\frac{1}{2}\) is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: Differentiate your answer: do you get back \(\frac{1}{2x + 1}\)?
